The word magpie has two main meanings — one literal (an actual bird) and one figurative (used to describe a certain type of person). Both meanings are connected, and once you understand the bird, the figurative meaning becomes obvious.

A magpie is a wild bird that belongs to the crow family. It is a medium-to-large bird, known for being noisy, clever, and visually striking.

What it looks like: The most common and well-known type — the Eurasian magpie — has bold black-and-white plumage with a very long tail. Its black feathers often show a beautiful blue-green shimmer in sunlight. It is an easy bird to recognize because of this sharp, high-contrast coloring.

Where it lives: Magpies are found widely across Europe, Asia, and parts of the Americas. They are adaptable birds and live comfortably near humans — in gardens, parks, farmland, and forests. They are not shy.

How it behaves: Magpies are famously loud and chatty. They produce a rapid, rattling, machine-gun-like chattering call that is hard to miss. They are also highly social birds and are often seen in pairs or small groups.

How intelligent it is: Magpies are considered one of the most intelligent animals on the planet. They can solve puzzles, use tools, remember faces, hold grudges, mourn their dead, and — remarkably — recognize themselves in a mirror. This last ability is extremely rare in the animal kingdom and is generally considered a sign of self-awareness.

The "shiny things" reputation: Magpies have a famous, centuries-old reputation for being attracted to glittery or shiny objects — coins, rings, foil, jewelry — and stealing or collecting them. This reputation is so strong that it has deeply shaped language and culture. Interestingly, scientific studies have actually questioned this stereotype, finding that magpies may even be cautious or wary of unfamiliar shiny objects. But the cultural image has stuck so firmly that it continues to define how people think and talk about magpies.

Superstitions: In British and European folklore, magpies are surrounded by superstition. A single magpie is considered bad luck; two magpies are good luck. There is even a famous rhyme counting magpies: "One for sorrow, two for joy..." — a tradition many people still follow today. In East Asian cultures, especially in China and Korea, the magpie is actually considered a lucky, joyful omen, symbolizing good fortune and happiness.

When the word is used to describe a person, it carries one or both of these meanings:

a) Someone who talks constantly and noisily
If you call someone a magpie, you are saying they talk too much — they chatter on and on, often about trivial things, rarely stopping for breath. This sense comes directly from the bird's noisy, incessant chattering call. It is mildly critical, suggesting the person is more talkative than necessary.

"Don't invite her to a quiet dinner — she's an absolute magpie. You won't get a word in."

b) Someone who collects random things
A magpie is also a person who picks up and hoards all sorts of objects — particularly things that catch their eye, often because they are shiny, pretty, or simply interesting. The person does not necessarily have a focused, organized collection; they simply accumulate things impulsively, a little the way the bird is imagined to do.

"His desk is a mess — he's a total magpie. There are old coins, buttons, broken watches, and random gadgets everywhere."

These two meanings can overlap. You might describe someone as a magpie because they both talk too much and collect random things.

Both figurative uses are gently unflattering but rarely harsh or cruel. Calling someone a magpie is more affectionate teasing than a serious insult. It implies a certain charming, impulsive, scattered quality — someone who is energetic and drawn to life's glittery corners, even if they lack focus or restraint.
4. The Word Used as a Modifier

You will also see "magpie" used as an adjective-like modifier to describe behavior:

  • "She has a magpie eye for beauty" — she has a habit of spotting and being drawn to beautiful or interesting things, the way a magpie is drawn to shiny objects.
  • "a magpie mind" — a mind that jumps from one shiny idea to the next, collecting many interests without going deep into any one of them.

SenseWhat it means

As a bird: a striking black-and-white, long-tailed bird known for intelligence, loud chatter, and a reputation for collecting shiny objects.

As a person: someone who chatters nonstop, or someone who compulsively collects random things (or both). The tone is gently teasing, not deeply insulting.

The figurative meanings both flow naturally out of the bird's two most famous traits: its noisy call and its legendary love of glitter.
